entry.summary:
Source: @sharenovate

✳️"The Night of the Dictator's Death"
We were always three: me, you, and "Him." "He" was always present—in the headscarves of women in movies at bedtime, in school textbooks, in the voices of the elegies that had taken over the streets. "He" was even more present in absences: in the absence of women's voices in our music, in the absence of watching a family football match at the stadium, in the absence of a homeland for millions of displaced people. Just as He was present in the absence of the thousands killed by His orders, at the celebration of His death.

And "The Night of the Dictator's Death" is the moment when He is no longer supposed to be everywhere. And it is precisely the morning after the dictator's death that, when we wake up, we know we are living in a different world—but we don't even know what that world looks like.

"He" is gone, but His shadow still looms over us. And all at once, we seem unable to forget that shadow. We have imagined this day so often as a wish that now the image of the world after His death keeps slipping away from our imagination.

"He" was present in everything and everywhere—all the surveillance cameras were His eyes. All the mobile phones were listening devices that seemed to be His ears. In a land that did not belong to "Him," He was everywhere. And His very presence was enough to keep us from talking more about His tomorrow. We had talked so little about His death that it had turned into a lump in the throat so large that we could no longer bear its joy.

"He" was gone, and the dance that had been aching inside us was turning into dance, into laughter, into a strange ambiguity in time.

"He" died, but war, violence, death—in a word, His shadow—still remains, still gaining strength. The bombs that drip from His words still take children's lives. The hatred He planted in this land is still gaining strength in the streets, and it is still hatred that spreads across the world.

We will hate "Him" forever, and no word can express that hatred. We still hate even His shadow—that shadow that seems to whisper from the depths of our hearts: "Are you sure the dictator is dead?"
@sharenovate

The book "The Saint of the Lowly" by Christian Bobin, the French writer and poet, is imbued with philosophical and mystical perspectives. In "The Saint of the Lowly," Bobin explores the themes of friendship and affection through a collection of short prose pieces. In this book, Bobin describes love as a stage of human evolution and takes the reader along on this journey.
Author: Christian Bobin
Translator: Farzaneh Mehri

entry.summary:
Source: @sharenovate

The Ashura of "Oppressed Iran"!
Ashura and the mourning of #Moharram are not merely a collective religious ritual; they are also the reaction and narrative of Iranian society about itself in every era. The reinterpretation of Ashura differs according to the characteristics of each time, and this affects its rituals.
It seems that the observance of Ashura rituals over the past 50 years has followed four completely different patterns:
1- Revolutionary Ashura (from the 1950s to 1979)
2- War Ashura (the 1980s)
3- Carnivalesque Ashura (the 2000s and 2010s)
4- The Ashura of Oppressed Iran (the 2020s)

entry.title: 🖋The Many Kinds of Artificiality of an Intelligence🧠 Every new product,…
entry.summary:
Source: @sharenovate

🖋The Many Kinds of Artificiality of an Intelligence🧠
Every new product, one step to life, one step to death!
🔸Amir Nazemi, a researcher, has written a note for "Shargh Daily" about the development of artificial intelligence by major tech companies, noting that developments in this field seem like an exciting movie to the public, but for tech and digital economy activists, it has become a lightning-fast (blitz) game of chess.
🔸In the rest of this note, he introduces Grok, the AI developed by X, and Helix, introduced by Figure AI, noting that these two AIs entered the scene a few weeks after all the hype around DeepSeek.
🔸In the final section of this note, he also addresses the challenges of AI development for Iranian startups. While enumerating these challenges, he believes that actors in the country's startup ecosystem should take future scenarios in AI development more seriously.
🔸In this regard, Nazemi has written: "The fact that the strategy of most actors in an ecosystem suffers from a strategic mistake indicates deeper roots of a wrong orientation in a society. Something I consider to be disconnection from the world, due to sanctions and filtering. But the main pain is that with the emergence of each product, the chance of success for Iranian startups decreases, even though they themselves are thrilled by these new products."
🔗 Read the full version of this note from the link below: https://www.sharghdaily.com/fa/tiny/news-974612
